content: The mucous membrane of the nose lines the nasal cavities and is closely attached to the underlying periosteum or perichondrium. It transitions seamlessly into the skin at the nostrils (nares) and connects with the mucous membrane of the nasopharynx through the posterior nasal apertures, also known as the choanae. The mucous membrane is also continuous with the conjunctiva via the nasolacrimal and lacrimal ducts, and it communicates with the frontal, ethmoidal, sphenoidal, and maxillary sinuses through various openings in the nasal meatuses. The membrane is thickest and most vascular over the nasal conchae and is also relatively thick over the nasal septum. However, it becomes very thin in the meatuses, on the floor of the nasal cavities, and within the sinuses. This tissue is one of the most frequently infected areas in both adults and children. Inflammation of the nasal mucosa can lead to significant symptoms, including nasal congestion, headaches, and mouth breathing, which can interfere with daily activities. The thickness of the mucous membrane narrows the nasal cavities, making the middle and inferior nasal conchae appear larger and more prominent than they do in the skeletal structure. Additionally, the openings that connect the meatuses to other structures are significantly reduced in size. The structure of the nasal mucous membrane varies depending on the functional region of the nose. In the respiratory region, the epithelium is composed of columnar, ciliated cells. Interspersed among these are goblet cells, which produce mucus, and smaller pyramidal cells located at the base of the epithelium. Beneath the epithelial layer lies a fibrous layer infiltrated with lymphocytes, forming diffuse adenoid tissue in many areas. Below this is a nearly continuous layer of glands, both mucous and serous, whose ducts open onto the surface of the mucosa. In the olfactory region, the mucous membrane has a yellowish hue, and the epithelial cells are columnar but non-ciliated. These cells are of two types: supporting cells and olfactory cells. The supporting cells have oval nuclei located in the deeper parts of the cells, forming a zone of oval nuclei. The superficial portion of each supporting cell is columnar and contains yellow pigment granules, while the deeper portion extends as a delicate process that interconnects with similar processes from adjacent cells, forming a network within the mucosa. Interspersed among these supporting cells are bipolar olfactory nerve cells. Each olfactory cell consists of a small amount of granular cytoplasm, a large spherical nucleus, and two processes. The superficial process extends between the columnar epithelial cells and projects onto the mucosal surface as a fine, hair-like structure called the olfactory hair. The deep process extends inward, often appearing beaded, and continues as the axon of an olfactory nerve fiber. Beneath the epithelium and throughout the thickness of the mucous membrane lies a layer of tubular, often branched glands known as Bowman’s glands. These glands are structurally similar to serous glands. The epithelial cells of the nasal mucosa, as well as those in the pharynx and respiratory passages, play a critical role in maintaining a stable temperature by keeping the surface slightly lubricated with moisture. The nasal mucous membrane is commonly affected during viral infections such as the common cold and influenza, leading to inflammation and associated symptoms.
